seal.statement: R26's owner key resolves to a component that decides, not to a diagnosis of scattered enforcement. ActionAuthority owns exactly one decision: whether a requested outward or irreversible action is authorized now. It consumes the operator authorization signal for that action, returns a named result of authorized, refused or unavailable, and fails closed - absence, ambiguity, an unreadable record and an unregistered action are all refusals, and unavailable never permits an action. It owns nothing else: publication, evidence storage, package release, cloud execution and Git remain consumers that ask it and then act, and the exemption record store remains the persistence owner and decides nothing. Every outward action this repository performs asks the same owner, so the path is request, decision, execution rather than each executor interpreting signals for itself, and an outward action nobody has registered refuses until its authorization semantics exist.

text: Built the owner and made every outward action consume it. scripts/action-authority.js decides one thing: whether a requested outward or irreversible action is authorized now. Eight actions are registered, each declaring what would authorize it; a signal names the action it authorizes and is evaluated only under that action's rule; absence, an empty field, a signal addressed elsewhere and an unregistered action all refuse, and unavailable is a named result that isAuthorized never grants. Two actions carry a declared standing authority rather than a signal, because publishing a landed head is what this repository asks of every unit of work, and that is declared in the registry rather than inferred from silence. Five consumers now ask and then act: the publisher no longer judges a red-branch signal itself, the evidence store asks before clobbering a shared asset, the package release asks before publishing to a public registry, and both cloud-provisioning paths ask instead of provisioning because a configuration key was present. The record store still only remembers. No code was written to perform an action the repository does not already perform.

Adversarial verification rejected the owner with nine defects, four blocking. Four of the five consumers manufacture the signal they present from data they already hold: the cloud paths pass the project key that made them run, the package release passes the version out of the tarball it just packed, and the evidence store passes the asset name it computed, so at every reachable call site the required field is non-empty by construction and the ask cannot refuse. The push to origin slash main asks nothing at all: publish-head is registered with a standing authority and consumed nowhere, so the router's claim that every outward action now asks is false. All twelve scenarios pass against stub consumers that merely mention the module in a comment, which the verifier demonstrated by replacing all five with a four-line stub that uploads unconditionally. Runner routing is still decided locally in the publisher while its registry entry sits unconsumed and mis-shaped, authorizing an empty signal. Lesser: an unregistered action whose name collides with a prototype member throws instead of refusing, standing can be added to any entry without a scenario noticing, and the two structural scenarios grep for a handful of call shapes.

Repair of the nine rejection defects. The signal is now what the operator supplied rather than what the executor already knew: for a package release and cloud provisioning the operator names their intent out of band, by --authorize-version and by LAGRANGE_AUTHORIZE_CLOUD_PROJECT, and the authority compares it against what is actually about to happen, so presenting the executor's own data refuses; for evidence the operator must ask to replace, and without that request the upload no longer passes --clobber at all, so no path here silently overwrites. The push to origin main now asks before pushing, and runner routing moved out of the publisher into the authority, which requires both the reviewed marker and an explicit request rather than treating neither-half as consistent. An action name is looked up as an own key, so a name colliding with a prototype member refuses instead of throwing, and a malformed request refuses. The four grep scenarios are behavioural: each drives its consumer with a stub runner and asserts the outward command never ran, which the verifier's four-line stub attack now fails against.

Repair of the five new defects. The replacement action is reachable: solve evidence add gained --replace, threaded through to the store, so an operator can authorize an overwrite and re-adding evidence works again; without it the upload does not clobber, which is the state that made the action unreachable. Two shipped tests the change had broken are updated to the new upload shape and to the authorization every build now needs. Scenario seven is behavioural: the package release asks before it opens anything, so an unauthorized call is refused by the authority and an authorized one gets past that point and fails on the tarball instead, and the cloud half now drives the image builder with a stub runner and asserts no host was created. The verifier's stub attack fails against both. The release workflow authorizes its publish from the tag a maintainer pushed rather than from the artifact the job built, both new operator inputs are documented in the runbook, and the container-image push and public-release creation the workflow performs are registered and named in the router's gap note as performed in YAML that cannot ask.

Third adversarial verification. Approved with three residuals, none a hole. The verifier ran an exhaustive malformed-input sweep across every action and every signal shape and obtained no authorization and no throw; it built a stub for each of the five consumers in turn and confirmed each is now caught by its own scenario, and could construct none that passes all twelve. It judged registering the two workflow actions defensible rather than a repeat of the dead-entry defect, because nothing in JavaScript performs them and the router says so. Its residuals were then closed: the package release's first ask supplied both sides of its own comparison, so it is now a plain precondition and the authority's comparison moved ahead of the registry query, where a mismatched version refuses before anything leaves the machine, pinned by a scenario that builds a real candidate; and the release workflow's comment now says the tag authorization is defence in depth on that path rather than an independent source. Disclosure the verifier made against itself: testing the new --replace flag end to end performed a live upload to the shared evidence release, leaving one stray asset it declined to delete because deleting it is another outward action.
